traces.question: The cross-section SEM panel (F1b) of the 475 nm Au film on fused silica. What does the panel show about how the grains sit through the film thickness, and what does that establish about the grains' shape?

This establishes that the grains are columnar: one grain runs the full film thickness, with boundaries going from the substrate to the surface (a10). traces.question: The panels F6a, F6b, F6c, F6d, F6e are the retrieved phase maps of the same embedded Au grain, one per step of the thermal cycle (starting at 50 C, rising through roughly 240 C, then cooling back down). Reading only these five maps and the setup context (no accompanying text), how does the strain heterogeneity rank across the five conditions and along which axes, and is the resulting diffraction-peak broadening actually strain rather than just a crystallite-size effect?
traces.answer_key: The phase maps are uniform along z (through the film thickness) at every temperature, so there is no ranking difference through the thickness. In the film plane the heterogeneity is y-dominated at 50 C, then breaks into jumps along x by 240 C, and largely returns to the low-temperature pattern on cooling (o13) -- so the ranking runs low anisotropy at low temperature to strongly x-concentrated anisotropy at high temperature, reversing on cooling. This is genuine strain, not a crystallite-size artifact: the size-only broadening computed for the grain is 6.61e-4 A^-1, two to seven times smaller than the measured qx widths (o12), confirming the qx broadening tracks real strain heterogeneity rather than grain-size resolution.
traces.grading: Independent channel o12 (DERIVED size-only broadening estimate, 6.61e-4 A^-1, two to seven times smaller than measured qx widths), held out from the model; used to confirm that the ranking read off o13 reflects genuine strain rather than a crystallite-size artifact.

traces.question: The study follows one buried Au grain through a full thermal cycle using 3-D coherent X-ray diffraction with phase retrieval. Panels F6a, F6b, F6c, F6d and F6e give the retrieved phase maps at successive points in that cycle. Comparing across these five panels, how does the intra-grain strain-heterogeneity pattern (along the film-plane axes versus through the thickness) change with temperature, and what happens to it once the sample is cooled back down?
traces.answer_key: Along the film thickness (z) the retrieved phase maps stay uniform at every temperature step. In the film plane the heterogeneity is dominated by the y-direction at 50 C, then breaks up into jumps along x by 240 C, and on cooling it largely returns to its original pattern (o13). traces.question: Intra-grain strain heterogeneity in the Au film is strongly anisotropic and grows with temperature: it develops along x in the film plane but stays weak through the thickness. The supporting evidence is: a cross-section SEM showing grains spanning the full film thickness with curved (not straight) boundaries; the qx peak width growing monotonically with temperature; the size-only broadening being two to seven times smaller than the measured qx widths; and retrieved phase maps that are uniform along z at every temperature but break into x-direction jumps by 240 C and largely return on cooling. Two candidate causes are on the table: the columnar grain shape (one grain spanning the whole film thickness), and thermal-loading defect storage that preferentially builds up along x where misoriented boundaries block transmission. What mechanism actually produces the observed x-direction growth, and why can the defect-storage cause not explain it on its own?
traces.answer_key: The x-direction growth is produced by a specific pathway: misoriented neighbouring grains g3 and g6, lying along x, accommodate stress at their grooved boundaries and trap defects there, building the x-direction heterogeneity (a18) -- this links the columnar grain-boundary geometry to defect trapping at specific x-oriented misoriented boundaries. The rival cause, thermal-loading defect storage alone (a14), cannot account for the optimum on its own: unlike the columnar-grain cause, no evidence establishes where a14's effect peaks, so by itself it cannot explain why the heterogeneity is strongest along x while staying weak through the thickness. Consistent with this, the heterogeneity's evolution is quasi-reversible on cooling, i.e. anelastic rather than a permanent plastic change (a17), a behavior recoverable because the method follows one buried grain through a full thermal cycle and returns both its average strain and its 3-D displacement field (a19). This supports the conclusion that a single grain carries large, anisotropic and quasi-reversible intra-granular strain heterogeneities set by its immediate neighbourhood, invisible to averaged diffraction (a20), and motivates the further hypothesis that 3-D coherent X-ray diffraction with phase retrieval on a single grain during thermal cycling should resolve the intra-grain displacement field and its reversibility (a2).
traces.grading: Judge against the graph's explaining mechanism (a18) as the key answer, with the cross-check that the rival cause a14 has no established optimum matching the claim a16's x-direction/through-thickness pattern; a17, a19, a20, a2 checked as the consistent downstream elaboration that must not itself be volunteered as the answer.
